question: If moving from 97% to 99% Dark Store availability requires 2 additional replenishment trips per day and increases transportation cost by 12%, what would the business prefer?

options.label: Accept the 12% increase - 99% availability is worth the additional cost.
Accept the increase only if 99% can be achieved consistently within the planned operating model.
Accept it only for high-value / high-velocity stores and critical SKUs.
Do not accept the increase unless the additional sales or margin generated covers the 12% cost.

question: A Dark Store is projected to stock out 90 minutes before its next planned vehicle. An additional trip would run at only 40% vehicle utilization. What should happen?

options.label: Send the vehicle - protecting availability takes priority over utilization.
Send it only if the situation crosses a predefined stockout/service threshold.
Send it if the affected products are critical or time-sensitive.
Wait for the planned trip unless the expected loss is greater than the cost of the additional trip.

question: If increasing replenishment from 3 to 5 trips per day improves availability by 1–2 percentage points but increases middle-mile cost by 8–10%, what is the preferred position?

options.label: Increase to 5 trips - higher availability is worth the cost.
Maintain 3 trips unless the additional frequency can be incorporated into a standardized operating cycle.
Increase frequency selectively for fast-moving or sensitive products/stores.
Increase frequency only if the incremental commercial benefit exceeds the incremental transportation cost.

question: A reefer vehicle costs 15% more than a standard vehicle but reduces temperature/freshness risk for FnV. How should the business view the premium?

options.label: Pay the premium whenever required; product integrity should not be compromised.
Pay it when required by defined product and temperature standards.
Pay it selectively for products where freshness materially affects customer value or shelf life.
Pay it only where the value of reduced spoilage / quality loss exceeds the 15% premium.

question: Peak-day demand can be 40% higher than average. Maintaining enough dedicated capacity for the peak would leave vehicles underutilized on normal days. What should the business prefer?

options.label: Maintain the peak capacity - protecting availability during peak periods is worth the normal-day underutilization.
Maintain capacity against a defined planning standard and handle exceptional peaks through controlled mechanisms.
Maintain additional capacity for critical stores/products and flex the rest.
Use flexible/spot capacity during peaks rather than carrying the cost of permanent excess capacity.

question: A replenishment vehicle can either depart at 65% utilization immediately or wait 45 minutes to reach 90% utilization. Which outcome is preferred?

options.label: Depart at 65% - inventory should move immediately.
Follow the planned dispatch window and utilization standard.
Decide based on the urgency and importance of the inventory being moved.
Wait for 90% utilization unless the cost of the delay exceeds the transportation saving.
